infra.matter_verdict: YES — specify Matter certification as your default purchasing filter in 2026, but treat it as a compatibility floor, not your integration layer. State of play: Matter 1.4 (Nov 2024) fixed the worst pain — proper multi-admin (one consent to share a device across Apple/Google/Alexa/SmartThings), energy device types (solar, battery, heat pump — relevant to your heat-pump-ready design), and better sleepy-device battery life. Thread 1.4 is the bigger win: since 1 Jan 2026 new border routers can ONLY certify against Thread 1.4, which mandates credential sharing — new border routers join your existing mesh instead of spawning rival networks. The 'five competing Thread meshes' folklore from 2023-24 is genuinely dead for new kit. Matter 1.5/1.5.1 (late 2025) added cameras and doorbells on paper. What genuinely works cross-ecosystem: lights, plugs, switches, thermostats, locks, blinds, contact/motion/temp sensors, robot vacuums — pair once, control from Apple Home AND Google AND Alexa simultaneously, setup under 2 minutes. What still does not: ecosystem implementation lag is the 2026 problem, not the spec. SmartThings ships full 1.5; Amazon Alexa was still effectively on 1.2 support in early 2026 (e.g. no Matter leak sensors); Google Home sits on partial 1.4 and still hasn't exposed generic switches — IKEA's Bilresa remote fails on Google, Klippbok leak sensor fails on Alexa. Matter cameras are spec-real but retail-immature — do NOT plan your CCTV around Matter; use PoE/ONVIF (see security). Practical spec for 115 Vicarage Road: every light relay, socket, TRV, sensor and lock you buy should be Matter-certified (Shelly Gen4, Aqara, Eve, Tado X class), your hub should be a Thread 1.4 border router, but run the house on a local hub (Home Assistant) with Matter as the buyer-facing handover layer, not the plumbing. That combination is exactly what survives 15 years: certified devices outlive any single ecosystem's app.
infra.wired_backbone: This is the single highest-leverage first-fix spend — copper in a cavity-masonry wall is nearly free now and near-impossible later. Spec CAT6a throughout (10GbE over full 100m channel, better PoE thermal headroom; UK installed cost £130-200/point, far cheaper as one first-fix job). RUN COUNT (~28-34 drops for 305m2/3 storeys): TVs — 2x CAT6a to each TV wall (main lounge by the 4.8m slider, snug/cinema, grandparents' sitting area, master): one for the TV, one spare/console; APs — 1x CAT6a to a CENTRAL CEILING position on each of the 3 floors (3 runs, consider a 4th to a rear soffit/garden-facing eave for outdoor Wi-Fi covering the robot mower); cameras — 1x to each of 4-6 external positions at soffit height: front covering the drive (busy road = your highest-risk zone, 2-3 cars), both side approaches, rear garden/slider; doorbell — 1x CAT6a to the front door at doorbell height (do this even if you fit a battery doorbell first — it future-proofs PoE doorbells forever); office — 2-4 drops; each teen bedroom — 1; utility/plant — 1 (boiler/heat-pump controls, UFH manifold zone controller); hallway — 1 at eye level for a future PoE wall tablet/intercom (PoE screens are real in 2026; PoE speakers remain commercial/niche — don't cable for them, conduit instead). Wi-Fi 7 APs: ceiling-mounted, central, one per floor (UniFi U7 Pro/Lite class, 2.5GbE, standard 802.3af/at PoE — golden rule is high and central, 20-30% overlap, never corners). Three ceiling APs will comfortably blanket 305m2 of masonry. CONDUIT/DRAW-STRING: 25mm flexible conduit with draw cords from the comms cupboard to (a) each TV wall — future HDMI/fibre as standards change, (b) the loft/crown-roof void — serves the electric stairhead rooflight controls and anything future, (c) an external soffit — future cable/fibre/camera additions, plus one oversized (50mm) vertical spine GF-to-roof. Conduit is the cheapest future-proofing that exists. FIBRE ENTRY: Openreach FTTP enters via an external CSP box and duct — have the builder lay the duct now (must be sealed against gas/water ingress; Openreach seal it permanently at install) and route it so the ONT lands IN the comms cupboard next to power, not in the hallway where engineers default to. Lay a SECOND duct to the boundary for a future altnet fibre — pennies now, a second provider forever. COMMS LOCATION: a ventilated cupboard (under-stairs or utility, NOT the airing cupboard — cool matters), 9-12U wall rack: patch panel, 1U cable manager sandwiched against a PoE switch (16-24 port, 2.5GbE on AP ports), ONT, router, mini-UPS; dedicated unswitched double socket on its own radial; since the house is dMEV anyway, add a passive vent or tie a small extract duct into it — PoE switch + NVR run warm 24/7.
infra.control_philosophy: The 2026 answer for a £700k mainstream-resale family home is a LAYERED system where every layer degrades gracefully to 'normal house': (1) WIRING LAYER — buyer-proof by construction: keep completely standard, nice-looking dumb switch plates (retractive/momentary where dimming) with smart relays BEHIND them. This is the retrofit-proof, buyer-proof choice and the 2026 consensus: Shelly 1/Dimmer Gen4 class (~£12-16/point, Matter-certified, local control, no cloud, no hub required, fits behind virtually any switch) or Aqara/Sonoff equivalents. Smart bulbs lose to relays in every hardwired position (switch cuts their power, they drop off the network — lamps only). Proprietary smart-switch fascias (glass touch panels etc.) read as gimmick at resale and die with their vendor. CRITICAL FIRST-FIX INSTRUCTION for your per-point electrician: loop NEUTRAL to EVERY switch position and fit 47mm deep back boxes throughout — UK lighting convention gives you switched-live-only at the switch, and retrofitting neutral later means chiselling masonry; at first fix it costs nothing and it is the one decision you cannot cheaply reverse. (2) BRAIN LAYER — Home Assistant on a Green/Yellow-class box (~£100): local-first, no subscriptions, connects to everything (Zigbee, Thread, Matter, Z-Wave, your boiler/UFH, dMEV, robot mower, rooflight rain sensor), and the Open Home Foundation is actively pushing it from enthusiast tool to consumer product; 2026.x releases added per-protocol panels and WebRTC camera streaming. (3) FACE LAYER — expose the house to Apple Home (and/or Google/Alexa) via Matter, because that is what your family and a NORMAL BUYER actually touch. Resale logic: a buyer inherits (a) switches that just work as switches with zero apps, (b) wired internet everywhere, (c) optionally a labelled HA box they can adopt or bin. Nothing bricks, nothing needs a dealer. Which is exactly why Control4/Crestron are wrong here: not dead as businesses, but dead FOR THIS BUDGET — Control4 realistic entry $15-50k, comprehensive installs low-to-mid six figures, dealer-only programming, and at a £700k Kings Heath exit a proprietary system is a survey-stage liability, not a premium. UK buyer research (Samsung/agents 2026) shows buyers pay a premium for smart features ONLY when practical, reliable and invisible — energy, security, heating — which is precisely the relay+HA+Matter stack. Budget: ~£12-16/relay point x ~30 points + £100 hub + your electrician's per-point labour ≈ under £1,500 for whole-house smart lighting that reads premium and sells safely.
infra.security: CAMERAS: PoE + local NVR is the settled 2026 answer — no cloud subs. Cameras now ship with onboard NPUs doing person/vehicle/package detection on-device, killing the last justification for cloud plans; local recording saves £50-140/yr per camera vs Ring/Nest/Arlo. Two sane stacks: UniFi Protect (zero licence fees, polished family-friendly app, needs a UniFi NVR/Dream Machine — pairs perfectly with the U7 APs and one vendor for the whole backbone) or Reolink PoE + Reolink NVR (cheaper, RTSP/ONVIF open, best Home Assistant citizen). 4-6 cameras: drive/front (priority — busy road, 2-3 cars), sides, rear/slider, garden. DOORBELL: wire it PoE at first fix. Reolink Video Doorbell PoE (~£100) is the 2026 value pick — 2K, 180° head-to-toe, microSD+NVR redundancy, RTSP/ONVIF/HA/Alexa/Google, £0/month; UniFi's PoE doorbell if you go all-Protect. Ring/Nest still paywall recording (£5-25/mo) — avoid on your no-subscription philosophy. LOCKS — UK reality check: smart locks are NOT automatically insurance-approved. Insurers (Aviva, Direct Line, AXA, LV etc.) require BS3621 mortice on timber doors and TS007 3-star anti-snap cylinders on multipoint/composite doors. The four locks that matter in the UK 2026 market: Yale Linus L2, Yale Conexis L2 (multipoint-native, professional fit recommended — handle-linkage misalignment causes wear), Ultion Nuki (3-star cylinder + smart, the strongest insurance story) and Nuki Smart Lock 4 (fits ON a euro cylinder, leaves the multipoint mechanism untouched — most reversible). Rule: keep the certified mechanical lock as the insurance-bearing device, add smart on top, and confirm with your insurer IN WRITING. For a house with grandparents half the year, keyless entry is genuine utility, not gimmick. ALARM: Ajax is the 2026 sweet spot — Grade 2 certified, 7-year sensor batteries, anti-jamming, but installer-channel: have it installed by an NSI or SSAIB approved firm to PD6662, which unlocks (a) home insurance discounts of roughly 5-15%, (b) eligibility for police URN response, (c) optional ARC monitoring (~£15-25/mo) you can add or drop. Pure DIY (Ring Alarm class) earns essentially no insurer credit. WHAT INSURERS ACTUALLY DISCOUNT IN 2026: certified NSI/SSAIB alarm (5-15%); leak-detection with smartphone alerts and ideally auto shut-off valves at washing machine/boiler/tanks (5-10% with approved systems — cheap Matter/Zigbee leak sensors + a motorised valve on the incoming main is a high-ROI add during first fix); documented BS3621/TS007 3-star locks (5-10% with some insurers). Cameras and smart locks per se rarely earn an explicit discount — treat them as deterrence and evidence, not premium reduction. Keep receipts, certificates and installation records for all of it.

energy.pv_battery: AUG 2026 PRICES: PV ~£1,400-1,600/kWp installed (MCS England average £1,565/kWp, April 2026); 4kWp £6.5-8.5k, 6kWp £8-11k. Batteries ~£500-800/kWh installed: Fox ESS 5kWh from ~£3.4k, GivEnergy 9.5kWh ~£5k, Sigenergy SigenStor £4.5-7.5k, Tesla Powerwall 3 (13.5kWh) £8.5-11.5k. 0% VAT holds until March 2027 - install before then. EXPORT: Octopus Outgoing Fixed cut to 12p/kWh in March 2026 (was 15p); Flux/Intelligent Flux CLOSED to new sign-ups since March 2026; floor SEG 4.1p. The 12p export era means self-consumption, not export, drives the economics - which suits a 7-person household perfectly. DC vs AC: building new = DC-coupled hybrid inverter (one inverter, ~97% vs ~93% round-trip, cheaper overall); Powerwall 3, GivEnergy All-in-One 2 (12yr warranty, best value), SigenStor (modular, DC EV-charging ready) are the 2026 shortlist. AC-coupling is a retrofit pattern - irrelevant here. CROWN ROOF: yes, the hidden flat centre works and it is the premium move for your "invisible, resale-friendly" brief. Flat-roof PV is permitted development if panels+frame protrude <0.6m (up to 1m in the current guidance formulations) and sit >=1m back from every roof edge - the hipped skirts give you that setback almost automatically, and nothing is visible from Vicarage Road. Use a ballasted low-tilt (10-15 deg) east-west system: no membrane penetrations, packs ~2x the panel count of south-only racking, yields ~85-95% of an optimal 35-deg south array in UK conditions - a 5-15% haircut that invisibility and zero planning risk easily justify. CRITICAL FIRST-FIX ACTIONS: (1) tell the structural engineer NOW to allow ~60-80kg/m2 dead load on the crown flat for ballast; (2) upgrade the flat-centre membrane spec (the array outlives a cheap felt); (3) run empty conduit from the roof void to the plant/consumer-unit position for DC strings and comms - pennies now, carnage later. PAYBACK (honest, family of 7, ~6,000-8,000kWh/yr): 6kWp + 10-13kWh battery ~£13-17k; high self-consumption plus smart-tariff arbitrage gives 6-9 years realistic (sources claim 5-8 for high-usage smart-tariff homes; flat-tariff/low-usage homes see 9-12). Battery alone on a flat tariff does NOT pay - it only works paired with the tariff automation below.
energy.tariffs_automation: 2026 LANDSCAPE: Intelligent Octopus Go is the workhorse - 7p/kWh across a smart-managed ~6h overnight window, typical EV-household saving £771/yr vs the standard variable tariff (Octopus data May 2025-Apr 2026, SVT ~26p/kWh). Agile remains the tinkerer's option (half-hourly pricing, occasional negative "plunge" events) and pairs with the open-source Predbat battery optimiser for the best returns, but IOG + the battery maker's native app captures 80-90% of the value with zero effort - the right call for your no-gimmicks brief. WHAT AUTOMATION ACTUALLY CAPTURES: (1) EV charging at 7p - the single biggest win, ~£175/yr for 10k miles vs ~£1,800 petrol; fully automatic via Ohme/Octopus API. (2) Battery arbitrage - charge at 7p overnight, run the house all day, export PV surplus at 12p: £450-700/yr for a 10kWh battery on a 3-bed, realistically £600-900 for your consumption. (3) Immersion/cylinder overnight at 7p - roughly at parity with gas (~6-7p/kWh) so it is resilience not profit while the boiler lives, but becomes real money post-heat-pump. (4) UFH screed preheat on cheap rate - skip while gas-fired (gas is already the cheap fuel); note it for the heat-pump era, when the GF screed becomes a free thermal battery. REALISTIC TOTAL for this family with EV + battery + PV vs doing nothing on a standard tariff: £1,500-2,500/yr all-in (of which the EV-vs-petrol swap is the majority); tariff automation on the house alone (battery + DHW) is £600-1,000/yr. One caveat: 7-person daytime occupancy (grandparents home) means high baseload - which strengthens the battery case and self-consumption, weakening nothing.
energy.ev: BEST VALUE 2026: Ohme Home Pro / ePod (~£900-1,000 installed) - deepest tariff integration (direct Octopus/OVO/British Gas APIs), the default if you charge on Intelligent Octopus Go. Zappi V2.5 (£800-1,500 installed) if you want native solar-surplus charging (Eco+ mode) and myenergi ecosystem with the battery; Hypervolt Home 3 Pro (~£950-1,200) is the design-led middle. Pod Point Solo 3S ~£800 budget floor. Honest take: with a DC-coupled battery system doing the solar optimisation, the Ohme's tariff automation beats the Zappi's solar party trick - buy the Ohme, save the difference. FIRST-FIX PROVISION (do this NOW, costs ~£100): lay 32mm duct with draw cord from the consumer-unit position to TWO points on the drive frontage (you have 2-3 cars - assume a second charger by 2030); pull 10mm2 6181Y/T&E or leave the duct empty - 6mm2 is adequate for one 7.4kW unit on a short run, but 10mm2 future-proofs voltage drop and a possible load-managed second unit for trivial extra cost. Reserve a 40A way in the new consumer unit; modern chargers have built-in O-PEN protection so no earth rod needed. DNO: installer notifies via ENA Connect Direct - in 2026 >80% are approved instantly and 95% within 5 days; the real first-fix job is confirming your supply NOW while groundworks are open: check for a looped service (shared with next door - common in Kings Heath Victorian stock) and get National Grid Electricity Distribution to unloop/upgrade to 100A single-phase during the build, when it is free-to-cheap and non-disruptive. With PV + battery + charger you may also trip the 60A+ load threshold where the DNO wants the fuse check anyway. BUSY-ROAD REALITY: mount the charger on the flank wall between the two parking bays, tethered 7.5m cable so it reaches either car without ever crossing the footway (Birmingham City Council does not permit trailing cables over the pavement - do not plan on street charging); enable PIN/app lock and cable-lock (opportunist unplugging happens on main roads), and put it inside the CCTV field. A socketed unit looks cleaner for resale; tethered is what a family actually uses.
energy.heating: WHAT PAYS BACK: (1) Weather compensation on the existing boiler - the cheapest real win: an outdoor sensor or OpenTherm-compensating control (£100-300) drops flow temperatures automatically and typically saves 5-15% of gas by keeping the boiler condensing; with your deliberately oversized emitters it works even better. Insist the boiler runs compensated from day one - it also proves the low-flow-temp design before any heat pump arrives. (2) Smart UFH zoning on the GF manifold - Heatmiser NeoStat/neoHub (or Wunda) with per-loop actuators: reported 8-26% savings vs dumb stats, and app control matters in a 3-storey house. BUT keep zones honest: 3-4 zones max (kitchen/living, snug, hall, grandparent room) - screed UFH is slow-response and micro-zoning is gadgetry that a future heat pump will actively hate. (3) Rad circuit: ordinary TRVs + a compensating room stat capture most of the value. Smart TRVs (Tado/Wiser, ~£50-70/rad) are a COMFORT buy, not a payback buy, in a house occupied all day by 7 people - fit them only on teen bedrooms that overheat/oversleep. (4) Hot water - your strongest smart case: 7 people = huge DHW draw. A Mixergy unvented cylinder (250-300L, roughly £2-2.5k bare, quoted bundles to ~£4.2k - shop this) heats only the volume needed (claims up to 40% DHW savings; expect a real 10-20%), does volumetric top-down heating for 5x faster reheat between teen showers, integrates smart tariffs natively, and comes in a heat-pump-coil version - buy that version and your cylinder survives the transition. (5) Solar diverter (myenergi Eddi ~£400-500): GADGETRY for you - the 2026 maths says divert only if export pays under ~12p/kWh; at Outgoing's exactly-12p, exporting at 12p beats displacing ~6-7p gas heat. Skip it; Mixergy's own PV integration covers the edge case later. HEAT-PUMP-READINESS CHECKLIST to leave in the house file: emitters sized for 45C flow (done - document it); 28mm primaries on main runs, 22mm elsewhere, full-bore routes with no microbore anywhere; UFH manifold with blending valve and pump suitable for 35-40C; external wall position reserved for the outdoor unit (condensate soakaway, 32A supply + control-cable duct already run at first fix); plant space for 300L cylinder + optional buffer/low-loss header; hydraulic design that can collapse to 1-2 zones; room-by-room heat-loss calcs from the M&E design printed and left behind (this alone saves the future MCS installer a survey and you a mis-sized quote); dMEV and trickle vents unaffected. Cost of the checklist at first fix: under £500. Cost of retrofitting it: thousands.
energy.water: LEAK DETECTION/AUTO-SHUTOFF: fit a whole-home shutoff on the rising main at first fix - it is a 30-minute job now. Two credible 2026 options: Hero Labs Sonic (ultrasonic, machine-learning flow signatures, auto-shutoff, legionella/freeze alerts; ~£300-400 device + fitting; sold via Amazon UK and Aquilar for trade) and Grohe Sense Guard (~£440-485, Aquablock burst shutoff, pairs with battery Sense pucks under cylinder/washing machine/bathrooms). INSURANCE 2026: the honest picture is that mainstream UK insurers reward the cheap end - LeakBot (£149, often FREE with Hiscox, Aviva, L&G, RSA, Covea policies including an annual engineer visit) - rather than giving big published discounts for Sonic-class valves; the real financial case is avoiding an escape-of-water claim (average ~£9k, plus excess and premium loading) in a 3-storey house where a top-floor leak trashes two ceilings. Belt-and-braces cheap layer: Surestop-style remote stopcock (~£60-100) and £15 water alarms under the cylinder and washing machine. With 7 occupants and grandparents, auto-shutoff-with-app is genuinely useful, not gimmick. SMART IRRIGATION: modest money, decent water saving on a meter - Hunter Hydrawise X2/HC (~£150-250, contractor-grade, weather-based, cuts outdoor use up to ~50%) or Gardena smart Water Control (~£100-150) for a simpler tap-timer approach. Design note for your robot-friendly lawn: irrigate BEDS with drip lines, not the lawn (UK lawns survive; drip and robots coexist, pop-up sprinklers and robot mowers fight). FIRST FIX: run a 25mm MDPE spur + duct (power/comms) to the garden, outside tap with double-check valve, and an outdoor socket at the robot-mower dock position.
energy.overheating: You already own the two expensive parts - the electric stairhead rooflight (with rain sensor) and the 4.8m slider - so this is a controls problem, not a spend problem. THE PHYSICS: 3 storeys + stairwell + high rooflight = a stack-ventilation chimney. Purge = open the rooflight at the top, open a low-level inlet at the bottom (slider or vent-locked rear window), and the stack pulls cool air through the whole house. Under Part O this is exactly the "adequate means of removing heat" strategy, and night purge realistically knocks 2-4C off next-day peak temperatures - free air-conditioning. AUTOMATION THAT WORKS: temperature sensor at the stairhead (hottest point) + outdoor sensor; rule = IF inside >24-25C AND outside cooler AND not raining, open the rooflight (the built-in rain sensor already covers the failure mode). Buy the rooflight actuator with a dry-contact/relay input or an open integration (Velux Active class) so a £50 relay or Home Assistant can drive it - avoid closed-app-only units. Hard-wire this: fused spur + sensor cable to the stairhead at first fix. BUSY-ROAD SECURITY REALITY: the rooflight is your safe night vent (unreachable); the slider is NOT left open at night on Vicarage Road - so spec at least one rear/upper window with secure vent-lock night positions as the low-level inlet, or laminated restricted-opening casement. BLINDS: physics says external shading beats internal every time - heat stopped outside the glass. The cheap-that-reads-premium answer on the slider is a fixed deep overhang/brise-soleil designed in NOW (zero moving parts, zero maintenance, blocks high summer sun, admits low winter sun); motorised external venetians/screens work but are £2-4k and a maintenance item - gimmick-adjacent for resale. Inside, hard-wired (not battery) motorised blinds on the slider and rooflight are a comfort/glare buy: run the cable pockets and fused spurs at first fix (£100 of cable) whether or not you fit motors on day one. Internal rooflight blinds barely fight overheating once heat is in - their job is glare and winter heat retention. Total automation spend beyond what you own: £300-800.

qol.ai_home:
VERDICT AUG 2026: The family-facing AI layer is finally real, but buy it as a SERVICE, not as infrastructure. Wire the house dumb-but-ready (you already have a per-point electrician - exploit it), and let the assistant be replaceable.

WHAT TO BUY INTO: Alexa+ launched in the UK 19 March 2026 (first market outside North America), free with Prime during early access, £19.99/mo otherwise, plus browser access since July 2026. In 2026 head-to-heads it wins on actual smart-home execution: it builds routines conversationally ("lights off downstairs when no motion after 11pm" - it writes the automation itself), handles multi-step commands reliably, and has per-person voice profiles. Google's Gemini for Home is the better conversationalist but still cannot create routines - a real limitation for a 7-person household. For this family: Alexa+ on Echo Show units (kitchen + grandparent suite + landing) is the pragmatic pick - you likely have Prime already, and it covers the four jobs you named: routines, room-to-room intercom/drop-in (genuinely useful in a 3-storey 305m2 house - beats shouting up two flights), elderly check-in routines (e.g. no kitchen presence by 9am -> notify your phones; scheduled video drop-in), and multilingual/bilingual household support for the grandparents. Echo Show is also the best big-button-free elderly interface: voice-first, video calls to family abroad, no menus.

LOCAL-LLM HUBS - REAL OR HYPE: Real, but hobbyist. Home Assistant's Assist pipeline with the Voice PE puck (~£55) plus a local LLM is a genuine private Alexa replacement for lights/scenes/climate in 2026 (2-4s latency; sub-second for built-in intents), but the honest consensus is the cloud assistants remain years ahead on polish, music, multi-room and family usability. Do NOT make a local LLM the family's primary interface; DO consider Home Assistant as the quiet integration glue underneath (it talks to everything and survives any vendor's death), with Alexa+ as the voice on top.

LONGEVITY RULE: Buy Matter/Thread-certified devices and mains-wired kit with a manual fallback; avoid anything that bricks when a cloud dies (see Wemo, Jan 2026). At first fix: neutral at every switch, CAT6 to AP/camera/doorbell points, and standard UK back boxes everywhere - that wiring outlives every assistant ecosystem and is what a 2030 buyer inherits happily.
qol.entertainment:
FIRST-FIX GOLD (do this now, costs pennies): run speaker cable (16/4 or 2x 16/2) from one utility/understairs "rack" cupboard to ceiling-speaker positions in kitchen, snug, family bathroom and outside the slider, plus CAT6 x2 to every TV position, each teen bedroom, and 3 ceiling AP points (one per storey). Fit the back boxes and blank the ones you don't use. Cable now is ~£1/m; retrofit later is chased walls.

WHOLE-HOME AUDIO: The 2026 value answer is WiiM amps on a shelf driving wired ceiling speakers - WiiM Amp/Amp Pro (~£300-380/zone) group natively for multi-room, do AirPlay 2/Chromecast/Alexa, and pair with £80-150/pair ceiling speakers for sound that reads premium. That's a 4-zone house for ~£1,600 vs £4,000+ Sonos. Sonos launched the Amp Multi in 2026 chasing exactly this install market, but the company is wobbly - the 2024 app debacle, then successive layoffs into 2026 hitting the app/UX teams - so do NOT build eight zones of your house on Sonos. One Sonos (or any) soundbar in the living room is fine and resale-legible. Teen-proof reality: every platform now does per-room grouping and individual Spotify/AirPlay streams; the fights are about volume, not tech - put the amps in a lockable cupboard.

TV/CINEMA AT SANE MONEY: For the living/snug, a 65-77in panel beats a UST projector for a family room every time in 2026 - USTs still lose in daylight, need an ALR screen to look right, and read as "enthusiast gear" to a normal buyer. LG C5/C6-class OLED is the 2026 default recommendation (perfect blacks, 4x HDMI 2.1 @ 120Hz for the teens' consoles); if the room is sun-flooded through the 4.8m slider, a bright mini-LED (Samsung QN90-class, or TCL/Hisense for the value play) is the better tool. Budget ~£1,300-2,000 for 65in OLED, and put the money saved into the wall: a recessed/flush mount, CAT6 behind the TV, and a deep conduit drop for cables = the "premium" look for £150.

WIFI/GAMING: Full-fibre + Wi-Fi 7 with WIRED backhaul is the 2026 spec: a PoE switch in the utility feeding 3 ceiling APs (TP-Link Omada/UniFi U7 class, ~£100-150 each) covers 305m2 over 3 storeys flawlessly; wired backhaul roughly doubles satellite throughput vs wireless mesh and kills gaming latency complaints. Hardwire the consoles and TVs on the CAT6 you ran. This is invisible, cheap at first fix, and quietly reads as a serious house to any surveyor-age buyer's kids.
qol.lighting_qol:
STRATEGY: Skip lighting-control SYSTEMS (Lutron/Rako/Control4 whole-house = £8-15k and unrecoverable at £700k). Instead buy lighting-control MOMENTS at first fix: separately-switched circuits + hidden LED channel + neutrals everywhere, then add £10-40 smart relays/dimmers (Shelly/Zigbee behind standard plates) only where scenes earn their keep. Standard-looking switches everywhere = resale-safe.

THE THREE MONEY SHOTS: (1) Entrance axis - a run of 2-3 small warm (2700K) downlights or a wall-wash on its own dimmed circuit, triggered dusk-to-dawn; (2) Stair drama - low-level LED plaster-in wall lights or a concealed handrail/stringer strip on a PIR night circuit: cheap, dramatic, and doubles as grandparent-safe night navigation on three storeys; (3) Kitchen island - pendants on a dimmer plus dim-to-warm strip under the island overhang and in the plinth. Dim-to-warm (2700K down to ~1800K as it dims, incandescent-style) is now a commodity 2-wire strip - no controller needed, just a 24V dimmable driver in an accessible void and a PWM/mains dimmer; strip ~£20-40/m, recessed aluminium/plaster-in channel ~£10/m. Specify driver ACCESS (in a cupboard, not buried in the ceiling) - that's the maintenance killer people miss.

BLINDS/CURTAINS 2026 - WHAT'S COMMODITY vs RIP-OFF: Commodity: retrofit motors (SwitchBot Curtain 3 / Aqara E1 at £50-90/window) and Ikea Fyrtur-class motorised roller blinds (~£130-180) - fine for teen bedrooms. Still a rip-off: made-to-measure premium motorised systems (Lutron Serena £200-400/window; a bespoke motorised curtain track for a 4.8m slider £800-1,500+). PLAY: for the slider, first-fix a fused spur and a generous curtain pocket in the ceiling detail, then hang a heavy-duty MANUAL track with quality full-height curtains - reads premium, glides fine, motorise later if you ever care. For the crown rooflights: order the manufacturer's own electric blinds WITH the rooflights at purchase (integrated, warrantied, one remote with the rain-sensor opener) - retrofit skylight blinds are the classic rip-off (£300-600 each aftermarket). Wire the spurs for all of it now regardless.
qol.maintenance_killers:
ROBOT MOWER: Wire-free RTK/vision is genuinely solved in 2026 - boundary-wire models are being phased out. For a Kings Heath garden, a £700-1,000 unit is the sweet spot: Segway Navimow i-series (£699-999, best app/AI avoidance) or Mammotion Luba Mini AWD (£999). Caveat: RTK needs sky view - with a 3-storey house shading the garden, prefer a vision/LiDAR hybrid (Segway i210, Mammotion Yuka Mini 2, eufy E15 class) which navigate without a satellite fix. First fix: outdoor socket at a flat, discreet dock spot, and - the single best robot-friendly move - a flush brick/porcelain mowing strip around the lawn so it cuts to the edge and you never strim.

ROBOT VACUUMS: One self-empty unit per main floor is the 2026 pattern (self-empty is standard now; £300-500 buys excellent - Roborock/Dreame mid-range; the £800+ mop-washing combos are nice-to-have for the GF only). First fix: a socket inside a plinth/understairs niche per floor so docks hide - reads premium, costs nothing now.

WINDOWS/GUTTERS: Your Pilkington Activ-class self-clean glass is real tech but not maintenance-free - rain does most of the work, expect an annual wash of sheltered panes; CRITICAL: silicone contamination kills the coating and is near-impossible to remove, so brief every trade during the build to keep sealant off the glass faces. Gutter guards: worth it only where trees overhang or access is dangerous - fit mesh guards on the 3rd-storey/crown-roof runs (where a cleaning visit costs real money) and skip them at ground-reachable level; they reduce but never eliminate cleaning. Spec deep-flow gutters on the crown roof.

FABRIC: Silicone render mostly self-sheds but budget a soft-wash every ~5 years on north/shaded elevations for algae (a few hundred pounds); brick at splash zones is the true zero-maintenance detail. EPDM: validated - 30-50yr life, maintenance is an annual sweep-and-inspect. Porcelain: validated - unsealed, non-porous, jet-wash once or twice a year. Both are the correct 2026 low-maintenance defaults.

WATER SOFTENER: NO. Birmingham is supplied from the Elan Valley (Welsh upland water) at ~73mg/L CaCO3 - officially soft/moderately soft, among the softest in England. A softener here is £1,000+ of pure waste plus servicing. Delete it; this advice is for the South East, not B14.

SMOKE/CO: You're already interlinked (required). What adds value: spec Aico 3000-series (or FireAngel equivalent) with the RF module + SmartLINK gateway so the interlinked system pushes phone alerts - landlord-grade, surveyor-recognised, no cloud dependency for the actual alarm function. Cautionary tale: Nest Protect is discontinued (First Alert SC5 is its official successor) - never make life-safety depend on a consumer cloud product.

GRANDPARENT TECH: Echo Show in their suite = voice-first everything, video calls, drop-in intercom, multilingual - no buttons to learn. Fall detection WITHOUT wearables is real but device-specific in 2026: Aqara FP2 (~£60) does fall detection only when CEILING-mounted - put one in their bathroom and bedroom; note the newer FP300 does presence but NOT falls. mmWave presence sensors also drive the killer QoL feature: automatic low-level night lighting on their route to the bathroom. Alexa+ check-in routines (no morning presence -> notify family) close the loop. Pair with the UFH per-room control they already have for a warm-floor, no-thermostat-fiddling suite.
qol.do_not_buy: THE 2026 FAD/RESALE-POISON LIST: (1) Proprietary whole-house control systems (Control4, Crestron, Loxone, full Lutron) at a £700k exit - they scare mainstream buyers, need paid dealers to change a lightbulb scene, and read as a liability, not a feature. (2) Any cloud-only smart device without local/manual fallback - 2026 has been a graveyard: Belkin Wemo cloud shut down Jan 2026, Nest Protect and Gen1/2 Nest Learning Thermostats stripped of smart features. Buy Matter/Thread or dumb+relay. (3) Whole-house Sonos (6-8 zones) - the app fiasco plus rolling layoffs through 2026 make a £4-5k bet on one wobbling company foolish; wired speakers + swappable amps carry zero ecosystem risk. (4) UST projector as the main family telly - still loses in daylight, needs an ALR screen, baffles normal buyers; OLED/mini-LED wins. (5) Water softener - Birmingham's water is soft; pure waste here. (6) Premium "smart" appliances (WiFi ovens, screen-door fridges) - the £500-1,000 premium buys software that's abandoned in 5 years and adds nothing at resale. (7) Motorised curtains/blinds on every window at £400-1,500/opening - wire the spurs, motorise only the rooflights (factory-fitted) and maybe the slider later. (8) In-wall tablets/control panels - dated in 5 years, leave a hole; use removable Echo Shows on stands. (9) Battery-gadget sprawl (dozens of battery sensors/cams) - a maintenance treadmill masquerading as convenience; you have a per-point electrician, wire things. (10) Fake-lawn "zero maintenance" temptation - a robot mower plus real turf reads far better at £700k in a family suburb. (11) Smart lock as the SOLE means of entry on the front door - fine as an addition, but keep a normal key cylinder for buyers, grandparents and insurers. General rule: anything whose smartness lives in an app of a single small company will not survive to your exit; anything that is copper, cable, channel, conduit and standards (Matter, PoE, CAT6, 24V LED) will.

killed: NOTE: the three dossier texts were not attached to this prompt; kills below are applied to the standard candidate set for these three research streams plus every double-count against the stated build spec.

DOUBLE-COUNT KILLS (already in the build spec, delete from every dossier): electric stairhead rooflight with rain sensor; dMEV extract fans + trickle vents (and any 'smart humidity fan' upgrade of them); self-cleaning glass on the crown roof glazing; oversized radiators / low-flow-temp design (that IS the heat-pump-readiness, do not buy it twice); UFH zone piping in the GF screed.
MVHR retrofit or 'MVHR-ready ducting' — the spec is dMEV + trickle vents by design; a 3-storey duct retrofit is a £6k-10k fantasy a 2030 buyer will never pay for. Dead, not even Ready-For.

Cloud-subscription security (Ring/Nest/Arlo ecosystems) — monthly fees forever, footage hostage to a US cloud, and by 2030 a buyer inherits nothing but a dead account. Killed in favour of PoE + local storage.
Whole-house proprietary lighting/control systems (Loxone, KNX, Lutron, Control4) — £8k-15k, installer-locked, reads as a liability not a feature at a £700k Kings Heath exit.
Smart bulbs throughout (Hue-everywhere) — leaves with the owner, confuses guests and grandparents, dies at the wall switch. Replaced by neutral-at-switch wiring + quality dumb dimmers.
Smart locks on external doors — battery/cloud failure modes, insurance ambiguity, teens lose fobs; a 3-star Ultion-class cylinder reads more premium to a surveyor.
Digital shower valves, smart taps, smart mirrors, smart toilet seats, in-ceiling multiroom audio — gimmick tier; zero resale weight in 2030, real servicing cost.

Perimeter-wire robot mowers and 'bury the boundary wire now' advice — obsolete folklore; 2026 mowers are RTK/vision wire-free (Navimow i-series verified below), so no first-fix wire is wanted, just a socket and a level lawn edge.
Cloud energy-monitoring subscriptions and app-locked 'smart consumer units' — keep a dumb CT-clamp provision instead.
Solar PV diverter (iBoost-type) bought now — there is no cylinder on a combi-fed system today; the diverter decision belongs with the future heat-pump cylinder, not this tender.
Buying the EV charger / battery / PV / heat pump hardware NOW with no EV and a working boiler — capital parked in depreciating kit; all four move to READY-FOR provisions.
Hydrogen-ready boiler swap talk — 2023 folklore; UK policy has moved to heat pumps (BUS extended to 2030, verified below).
first_fix_now: Cat6 star-wired data points x ~16, all home-run to one patch position (understairs/plant cupboard): 3 teen bedrooms + study/WFH (1-2 each), living TV wall x2, kitchen, grandparents' room, 2 ceiling AP positions (GF + FF hallway), 4 camera positions at soffits (front x2 covering the busy-road drive, side, rear/garden), 1 doorbell drop. ~£120-180 of cable/boxes in materials, £50-75/point labour at open-frame first fix vs £90-200/point + up to 40% retrofit premium later (verified). Budget ~£900-1,200 total. This is the single highest-leverage line in the tender.

25mm conduit + draw cords to every 'later' location: twin runs loft-void-to-plant-cupboard for future PV DC/AC strings, front elevation drop for doorbell/camera, TV wall chase with recessed AV/brush plate. ~£100-150 materials; the same routes cost £500+ in redecoration after plastering.

EV provision: 6mm2 (or 10mm2 if the run is long) cable or capped duct from the consumer unit to the drive-side front wall + a reserved 32A way + space for an O-PEN device. ~£80-150 now; verified that a long cable run/CU work adds £150-450 to a later install on top of the £875-1,500 charger job.

PV + battery provision: 4 spare ways in a larger-than-needed consumer unit, AC isolator position in plant cupboard, labelled conduit ends in the loft, floor space (~1m x 0.4m) and ventilation in the plant cupboard for a battery. ~£60-120 delta on the CU order.

Heat-pump readiness (the cheap remainder): 28mm pipe sleeves through the external wall to a marked outdoor-unit pad zone, power + fused spur provision and a 1.9m tall footprint reserved for a future cylinder (airing cupboard/garage corner), UFH manifold wired for zone stats. ~£100-200. The rads and UFH already do the heavy lifting.
Neutral at every switch drop + 35/47mm deep back boxes throughout — a spec sentence, ~£0-100 delta, and it makes every future smart-switch/dimmer a 10-minute swap instead of a chase.

Hard-wired alarm first fix: PIR positions to corners of GF rooms + door contacts + bell-box cable, back to plant cupboard. ~£150-250 in cable/labour now; a wired Grade 2 system reads premium to insurers and buyers vs stick-on battery kit.
Robot-mower + garden services: external RCD socket at the rear (mower dock) + 32mm duct under the patio/path to the far garden corner (future garden room: SWA + Cat6). ~£80-120.
CT-clamp/monitoring provision: one Cat6 + 20mm conduit from meter position to plant cupboard. ~£20.
Doorbell: PoE Cat6 to door frame height with a deep back box — kills any future need for a battery/cloud doorbell. (Counted in the 16 points.)
fit_at_completion: Network head-end: small patch cabinet, 8-16-port PoE switch, 2x ceiling Wi-Fi 6E/7 APs — ~£450-600. Five residents + WFH + grandparents' video calls across 3 storeys of cavity masonry; this is what makes every other item work and it stays with the house.

PoE security, zero subscription: Reolink PoE video doorbell + 3-4 PoE cameras + NVR with local storage — ~£550-750 total. Verified no-monthly-fee, on-device person/vehicle detection, local recording; covers the 2-3 cars on a busy road, viewable by grandparents on a wall tablet without any cloud account.

Heating controls: wired programmable stats per UFH zone + a heat-pump-compatible dual-channel programmer for the rad circuit (Heatmiser Neo-class, local-first) — ~£350-500. Room-by-room comfort for grandparents without touching the boiler-to-heat-pump swap later.
Quality dumb dimmers + PIR external lighting on drive and rear — ~£250-300. Reads premium at viewings, nothing to pair, nothing to fail.
Wired alarm panel + Grade 2 kit on the first-fixed loops — ~£300-450 (self-managed, no monitoring contract).

Leak sensors (Zigbee, local hub) under kitchen sink / washing machine / UFH manifold + labelled accessible stopcock — ~£60-100. Screed UFH makes a slow leak the most expensive quiet failure in the house.

Segway Navimow i105E wire-free RTK+vision robot mower — £678-749 (verified UK 2026 pricing). The lawn is already robot-friendly; this is the family's weekly-hour dividend. Note: chattel — it leaves with Mo at sale.
Optional local hub (Home Assistant Green, ~£90) to tie stats/sensors/cameras together with zero cloud dependency — also a chattel; the house must work perfectly without it.
ready_for: Solar PV (~5-6kWp on the main roof) + inverter: provision now = labelled loft-to-plant conduits, spare CU ways, isolator position (~£60-120). Later spend ~£5,500-8,000. Warm Homes Plan-era grants/0% finance routes exist via local authorities for eligible homes — check at purchase time.

Home battery (~10kWh): provision now = plant-cupboard floor space, ventilation, reserved CU way (~£0-50 if planned into the cupboard). Later spend ~£3,000-5,000, ideally bought with the PV for one scaffold/one commissioning visit.

Heat pump: provision now = sleeves, pad zone, cylinder footprint, wired zone controls (~£100-200; oversized rads + UFH already in spec). Later spend: typical £11k-13k install minus verified £7,500 Boiler Upgrade Scheme grant (still live Aug 2026, scheme extended to 2030, and the old EPC insulation-recommendation blocker has been removed) = ~£3,500-5,500 net when the existing boiler dies.

EV charger: provision now = duct/cable + 32A way (~£80-150). Later spend £875-1,500 installed (Ohme Home Pro ~£999; Zappi £1,200-1,500 if PV fitted first — its solar diversion then earns its premium). No OZEV grant for homeowner houses, so the avoided £150-450 of retro cable work is real money.
Garden room / office: provision now = 32mm SWA duct + Cat6 duct under the path (~£80). Later spend £8k-25k structure — buyer-attractive at exit even if never built, because the duct is provable.
Second EV / load management: covered by choosing 10mm2 on the drive run now (£20 delta) instead of a second dig later.
Explicitly NOT ready-for: MVHR (spec'd out permanently) and any proprietary control system — no provision made, by design.
verdict.resale_philosophy: Sell the copper, keep the cloud: everything dumb, wired and in the walls (Cat6, conduits, ducts, PoE cameras-as-fixtures, spare CU ways, sleeves and pads) conveys with the house as 'future-proofed, no subscriptions' — everything with a login, a battery or an app account (mower, hub, NVR archive, EV charger if fitted late) leaves with Mo, and the house must work perfectly the day it leaves.
